summary.text: The truncated Catalan sum is rewritten by a difference-of-binomial identity as \(U(A,B)=[x^A]g(x)(1+x)^B\), where \(B=A(m+2)\) and \(g(x)=(1-x)^2(1+x)/(1-x^3)\). Expanding \((1+x)^p=1+x^p+p\Phi_p(x)\), divisibility of \(\Phi_p\) by \(1+x+x^2\) kills the first two correction terms, while anti-palindromic pairing and binomial/factorial \(p\)-adic valuation bounds give the required power of \(p\) for all later terms; integer-valued polynomial interpolation then extends the result to arbitrary integer \(B\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(x)=\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}=1+x+2x^2+5x^3+\cdots .
\]
We prove the slightly more general statement asserted in the OEIS comment. For every integer \(m\), let
\[
 a_m(N)=\sum_{j=0}^{N}[x^j]c(x)^{mN}.
\]
Then, for every prime \(p\geq 5\), every \(n>0\), and every \(k>0\),
\[
 a_m(np^k)\equiv a_m(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}.                 \tag{1}
\]
The sequence A333096 is the case \(m=4\).

Throughout, for an integer \(z\) and a nonnegative integer \(j\), write
\[
 {z\choose j}=\frac{z(z-1)\cdots(z-j+1)}{j!}.
\]
This is an integer, including when \(z<0\), and it obeys Pascal's identity in the usual form.

## 1. Rewriting the truncated Catalan sum

The standard Lagrange-inversion formula for powers of the Catalan series is
\[
 [x^j]c(x)^r=\frac r{r+j}{r+2j-1\choose j}\qquad(j>0),        \tag{2}
\]
with constant coefficient \(1\). A form which remains meaningful even when the displayed denominator vanishes is
\[
 C(r,0)=1,
 \qquad
 C(r,j)={r+2j-1\choose j}-{r+2j-1\choose j-1}\quad(j>0).     \tag{3}
\]
Indeed,
\[
 j{N\choose j}=(N-j+1){N\choose j-1}.
\]
Putting \(N=r+2j-1\), one obtains
\[
 (r+j)\left({N\choose j}-{N\choose j-1}\right)
   =r{N\choose j},                                           \tag{4}
\]
so (3) equals (2) whenever \(r+j\ne0\). Formula (3) is the actual formal-power-series coefficient in all cases.

Define the mathematically correct truncated sum
\[
 A_m(N)=\sum_{j=0}^{N}C(mN,j),
\]
with \(A_m(0)=1\). For the OEIS sequence, and more generally for every \(m\ne-1\), this is exactly the sum obtained from (2). There is one harmless issue if one defines (2) by integer division at a zero denominator. When \(m=-1\), the sole exceptional summand is \(j=N\): integer division gives \(0\), whereas (3) gives
\[
 {N-1\choose N}-{N-1\choose N-1}=0-1=-1.
\]
Thus, for every \(N>0\), the integer-division version and the true power-series version differ by the same constant \(1\). Consequently, any congruence between two positive indices proved for \(A_m\) also holds for the sequence as given by that integer formula. We shall therefore prove (1) for \(A_m\).

Introduce the periodic sequence
\[
 g_0=1,
 \qquad
 g_j=\begin{cases}2,&3\mid j,\\-1,&3\nmid j,
 \end{cases}\qquad(j>0).                                    \tag{5}
\]
Its generating function is
\[
 g(w)=\sum_{j\ge0}g_jw^j
     =\frac{(1-w)^2(1+w)}{1-w^3}
     =\frac{1-w^2}{1+w+w^2}.                                 \tag{6}
\]
For \(s\ge0\) and \(z\in\mathbb Z\), set
\[
 U(s,z)=[w^s]g(w)(1+w)^z
       =\sum_{j=0}^{s}g_j{z\choose s-j}.                     \tag{7}
\]
We next establish the key identity
\[
 A_m(N)=U\bigl(N,N(m+2)\bigr).                               \tag{8}
\]

Here is an elementary proof. Pascal's identity, together with the fact that every three consecutive positive \(g_j\)'s sum to zero, gives, for \(s>0\),
\[
 U(s,Z)-U(s-1,Z-2)
 ={Z-1\choose s}-{Z-1\choose s-1}.                           \tag{9}
\]
To see this directly, reindex (7) as
\[
 U(s,Z)=\sum_{q=0}^{s}g_{s-q}{Z\choose q}.
\]
Expand
\[
 {Z\choose q}={Z-2\choose q}+2{Z-2\choose q-1}+{Z-2\choose q-2}.
\]
The coefficient multiplying each interior \({Z-2\choose q}\) is a sum of three consecutive \(g\)'s and hence vanishes. The two boundary contributions are precisely the right side of (9). This also checks the small cases \(s=1,2\).

Now use induction on \(N\). On replacing \(Z\) in (9) by \(r+2N\), one gets
\[
 U(N,r+2N)-U(N-1,r+2N-2)
 ={r+2N-1\choose N}-{r+2N-1\choose N-1}=C(r,N).
\]
Starting from \(U(0,r)=1\), summing these differences proves
\[
 \sum_{j=0}^{N}C(r,j)=U(N,r+2N).
\]
Taking \(r=mN\) proves (8).

Thus the theorem will follow from a two-variable congruence for \(U\).

## 2. A cancellation modulo residue classes mod 3

Let \(p\ge5\) be prime. Since \(p\ne3\), multiplication by \(p\) preserves divisibility by \(3\), and hence
\[
 g_{pj}=g_j.                                                  \tag{10}
\]
For \(0<j<p\), define
\[
 \phi_j=\frac1p{p\choose j}\in\mathbb Z,
\qquad \phi_0=\phi_p=0,
\]
and put
\[
 \Phi_p(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\phi_jw^j.
\]
Then
\[
 (1+w)^p=1+w^p+p\Phi_p(w).                                   \tag{11}
\]

We require the following exact cancellation:
\[
 [w^{pM}]g(w)\Phi_p(w)=0\qquad(M\ge0).                       \tag{12}
\]
For \(M=0\) this is immediate. Suppose \(M>0\). Multiplying the desired equality by \(p\), it is enough to prove
\[
 \sum_{j=1}^{p-1}{p\choose j}g_{pM-j}=0.                    \tag{13}
\]
For a positive integer \(q\), formula (5) can be written
\[
 g_q=-1+3\,\mathbf 1_{3\mid q}.
\]
Since \(j<p\le pM\), we have
\[
 3\mid pM-j\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad j\equiv pM\pmod3.
\]
Thus the left side of (13) is
\[
 -\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}{p\choose j}
 +3\sum_{\substack{1\le j\le p-1\\j\equiv pM\ (3)}}{p\choose j}.       \tag{14}
\]
The first sum is \(2^p-2\). Each of the three interior residue-class sums in the second term equals \((2^p-2)/3\), so (14) is zero.

For completeness, that residue-class assertion is elementary. If
\[
 R_r(N)=\sum_{\substack{0\le j\le N\\j\equiv r\ (3)}}{N\choose j},
\]
then Pascal's identity gives
\[
 R_r(N+1)=R_r(N)+R_{r-1}(N).
\]
Induction, or the third-root-of-unity filter, gives
\[
 3R_r(N)=2^N+\epsilon_r(N),                                  \tag{15}
\]
where the correction is periodic of period six and takes values among
\(2,1,-1,-2,-1,1\), with a cyclic shift depending on \(r\). A prime \(p\ge5\) is congruent to \(1\) or \(5\pmod6\). Subtracting the endpoint terms \(j=0,p\) from (15), in each of the three residue classes the correction and the removed endpoints combine to \(-2\). Hence every interior sum is \((2^p-2)/3\), as claimed. This proves (12).

A second useful elementary identity is
\[
 U(N,2N)=1.                                                   \tag{16}
\]
Indeed, apply (9) with \(Z=2N\). The two binomial coefficients on its right are equal by symmetry, so \(U(N,2N)=U(N-1,2N-2)\), and induction reduces to \(U(0,0)=1\).

## 3. The first prime step

Put
\[
 Y=w^p+p\Phi_p(w).
\]
By (11), for a nonnegative integer \(B\),
\[
 (1+w)^{pB}=(1+Y)^B.
\]
Expanding by the binomial theorem and then expanding \(Y^t\), one obtains
\[
 U(pA,pB)
 =\sum_{t=0}^{B}p^t{B\choose t}
   \sum_{M=0}^{A}h_t(M){B-t\choose A-M},                    \tag{17}
\]
where
\[
 h_t(M)=[w^{pM}]g(w)\Phi_p(w)^t,
 \qquad h_0(M)=g_M.                                         \tag{18}
\]
The equality for \(h_0\) uses (10). The term \(t=0\) in (17) is exactly \(U(A,B)\).

We have
\[
 h_1(M)=0                                                    \tag{19}
\]
by (12). We also have
\[
 h_2(M)=0.                                                   \tag{20}
\]
Degree considerations make (20) automatic except possibly at \(M=1\): \(g\Phi_p^2\), after cancellation of its denominator as described below, has degree below \(2p\), and its constant coefficient is zero. For \(M=1\), insert \(A=1,B=2\) in (17). The left side is \(U(p,2p)=1\) by (16). The \(t=0\) term is \(U(1,2)=1\), and the \(t=1\) term vanishes by (19). Therefore the remaining possible term is \(p^2h_2(1)=0\), so \(h_2(1)=0\).

It follows from (17) that every term other than \(t=0\) is either zero, for \(t=1,2\), or contains \(p^t\) with \(t\ge3\). Therefore
\[
 U(pA,pB)\equiv U(A,B)\pmod {p^3}                            \tag{21}
\]
for nonnegative \(A,B\).

We need (21) also for arbitrary integer \(B\). We record a standard finite-difference interpolation argument. For fixed \(A\), \(U(A,B)\) is an integer-valued polynomial in \(B\), of degree at most \(A\), because it is a linear combination of the polynomials \({B\choose j}\). Hence
\[
 F(B)=U(pA,pB)-U(A,B)
\]
is an integer-valued polynomial of degree at most \(pA\). If an integer-valued polynomial \(F\) of degree at most \(d\) is divisible by an integer \(q\) at every nonnegative integer, then it is divisible by \(q\) at every integer. Indeed, its Newton expansion is
\[
 F(X)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}\Delta^jF(0){X\choose j}.                \tag{22}
\]
Each forward difference \(\Delta^jF(0)\) is an integral linear combination of \(F(0),\ldots,F(j)\), so it is divisible by \(q\); and \({B\choose j}\in\mathbb Z\) for every integer \(B\). Applying this to (21) gives
\[
 U(pA,pB)\equiv U(A,B)\pmod {p^3}                            \tag{23}
\]
for all \(B\in\mathbb Z\).

By (8), with \(B=n(m+2)\), (23) already proves
\[
 A_m(np)\equiv A_m(n)\pmod {p^3}.                            \tag{24}
\]
This is the case \(k=1\).

## 4. Anti-reciprocity and pairing

For higher prime powers we need more divisibility from the inner sum in (17). Let
\[
 \Phi_p(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}\phi_jw^j.
\]
The symmetry \({p\choose j}={p\choose p-j}\) shows that \(\Phi_p\) is reciprocal of formal degree \(p\). Moreover, (12), equivalently the equality of the three mod-\(3\) coefficient sums, implies that \(1+w+w^2\) divides \(\Phi_p(w)\) in \(\mathbb Z[w]\). Write
\[
 \Phi_p(w)=(1+w+w^2)Q_p(w).                                 \tag{25}
\]
The quotient has zero constant term, degree at most \(p-3\), and is reciprocal of formal degree \(p-2\).

Using (6) and (25), for \(t\ge1\),
\[
 g(w)\Phi_p(w)^t
 =(1-w^2)(1+w+w^2)^{t-1}Q_p(w)^t=:H_t(w).                   \tag{26}
\]
Thus this is a polynomial of degree at most \(t(p-1)\). The factors \(1+w+w^2\) and \(Q_p\) are reciprocal, while \(1-w^2\) is anti-reciprocal. Hence
\[
 w^{tp}H_t(1/w)=-H_t(w).                                    \tag{27}
\]
In terms of (18), (27) says
\[
 h_t(t-M)=-h_t(M)\qquad(0\le M\le t).                       \tag{28}
\]
Also \(h_t(0)=0\), because \(Q_p(0)=0\), and \(h_t(M)=0\) for \(M\ge t\) by the degree bound. At the midpoint, when \(t\) is even, (28) gives \(h_t(t/2)=0\).

Consequently, whenever \(t-1\le A\), the inner sum in (17) can be paired as
\[
\begin{aligned}
 &\sum_{M=0}^{A}h_t(M){B-t\choose A-M}\\
 &\quad=\sum_{\substack{1\le M\le t-1\\2M<t}}
 h_t(M)\left
overbrace{{B-t\choose A-M}-{B-t\choose A-(t-M)}}^{D_M}\right).             \tag{29}
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus it remains to estimate the binomial difference \(D_M\).

## 5. Binomial-difference estimates

We state and prove the estimates in the precise form needed below. Let \(r>0\), \(\alpha,\beta\ge1\), \(3\le t<p^r\), and \(1\le M<t/2\). Set
\[
 N=p^r\beta-t,
 \quad K_1=p^r\alpha-M,
 \quad K_2=p^r\alpha-(t-M),
 \quad \delta=t-2M.
\]
Then \(K_1=K_2+\delta\). The standard ratio identity
\[
 {N\choose K_1}\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(K_2+j+1)
 ={N\choose K_2}\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(N-K_2-j)             \tag{30}
\]
holds for generalized binomial coefficients as well. Put
\[
 Q=\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(K_2+j+1),
 \qquad P=\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(N-K_2-j).
\]
After reindexing the factors,
\[
 Q=\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(p^r\alpha-(M+j)),
\]
and
\[
 P=\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(p^r(\beta-\alpha)-(M+j)).
\]
Therefore
\[
 Q\left({N\choose K_1}-{N\choose K_2}\right)
 ={N\choose K_2}(P-Q).                                      \tag{31}
\]
Since the polynomial \(\prod_{j=0}^{\delta-1}(X-(M+j))\) takes congruent values at arguments congruent modulo \(p^r\),
\[
 p^r\mid P-Q.                                                \tag{32}
\]

If \(t\le p\), every factor of \(Q\) is prime to \(p\), because
\(1\le M+j<t\le p\). Kummer's theorem gives
\[
 p^r\mid {p^r\beta-t\choose p^r\alpha-(t-M)}.               \tag{33}
\]
Indeed, for every \(i=1,\ldots,r\), subtraction of the positive number \(t-M<p\) from a multiple of \(p^r\) produces a carry at the \(p^i\)-place; hence there are at least \(r\) carries in Kummer's formula. Equations (31)–(33), followed by cancellation of the factor \(Q\) prime to \(p\), give
\[
 p^{2r}\mid
 {p^r\beta-t\choose p^r\alpha-M}
 -{p^r\beta-t\choose p^r\alpha-(t-M)}.                     \tag{34}
\]
If the lower index exceeds the upper one, both this argument and the conclusion remain valid because the relevant ordinary binomial coefficient is zero.

For the middle range \(p<t<p^r\), define
\[
 \kappa=\#\{i:1\le i\le r,\ t\le p^i\},
 \qquad f=v_p((t-2)!).
\]
Kummer's theorem now gives at least \(\kappa\) carries, namely one at every level \(i\) for which \(t\le p^i\), and hence
\[
 p^\kappa\mid {N\choose K_2}.                               \tag{35}
\]
To spell out the carry: modulo \(p^i\),
\[
 K_2\equiv p^i-(t-M),
 \quad N-K_2\equiv p^i-M,
\]
so their least nonnegative residues have sum \(2p^i-t\ge p^i\). Thus a carry occurs.

Equations (31), (32), and (35) show that \(p^{\kappa+r}\) divides \(Q D_M\). The factors of \(Q\) have the same \(p\)-adic valuations as \(M,M+1,\ldots,M+\delta-1\), because each of these positive integers is below \(t<p^r\). This interval lies in \([1,t-2]\), so
\[
 v_p(Q)\le v_p((t-2)!)=f.
\]
After cancellation,
\[
 p^{\kappa+r-f}\mid D_M.                                   \tag{36}
\]
This proves all binomial-difference estimates used below.

We also need the elementary estimates for the outside binomial coefficient:
\[
 p^{r-v_p(t)}\mid {p^r\beta\choose t}\qquad(0<t<p^r),        \tag{37}
\]
\[
 p^r\mid {p^r\beta\choose t}\quad(0<t<p),                  \tag{38}
\]
and
\[
 p^{r-1}\mid {p^r\beta\choose p}.                           \tag{39}
\]
For (37), compare valuations in
\[
 t!{p^r\beta\choose t}
 =\prod_{j=0}^{t-1}(p^r\beta-j).
\]
The \(j=0\) factor contributes at least \(r\), and for \(0<j<t<p^r\),
\(v_p(p^r\beta-j)=v_p(j)\). Cancelling the valuations of
\((t-1)!\) leaves at least \(r-v_p(t)\). Formula (38) is its special case, and (39) follows similarly, with the single factor \(p\) in \(p!\) costing one power of \(p\).

## 6. The higher two-variable lift

We prove that for \(r\ge1\) and nonnegative \(A,B\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
&U\bigl(p(p^rA),p(p^rB)\bigr)-U(p^rA,p^rB)\\
&\hspace{35mm}\equiv0\pmod {p^{3(r+1)}}.                    \tag{40}
\end{aligned}
\]
If \(A=0\), both terms are \(1\). If \(B=0\) and \(A>0\), (7) gives \(U(s,0)=g_s\); then the two terms are equal by (10). Hence assume \(A,B\ge1\), and put \(A'=p^rA\), \(B'=p^rB\).

Use expansion (17) with \(A',B'\). The \(t=0\) term is \(U(A',B')\), so the difference in (40) is a sum, for \(1\le t\le B'\), of
\[
 T_t=p^t{B'\choose t}
 \sum_{M=0}^{A'}h_t(M){B'-t\choose A'-M}.                   \tag{41}
\]
We show that every \(T_t\) is divisible by \(p^{3(r+1)}\).

* If \(t=1\) or \(2\), the inner sum is zero by (19)–(20).

* If \(t\ge3(r+1)\), the explicit factor \(p^t\) suffices.

It remains to consider
\[
 3\le t<3(r+1).                                               \tag{42}
\]
The inequality \(t-1\le A'=p^rA\) holds, so pairing (29) is available.

First suppose \(t\le p\). By (34), the inner sum in (41) is divisible by \(p^{2r}\). If \(t<p\), (38) contributes another \(p^r\), so the total exponent is at least
\[
 t+r+2r\ge3(r+1),
\]
because \(t\ge3\). If \(t=p\), (39) contributes \(p^{r-1}\), and the total exponent is
\[
 p+(r-1)+2r\ge3(r+1)
\]
because \(p\ge5\).

Now suppose \(p<t<3(r+1)\). This case forces \(r\ge2\). The elementary inequality
\[
 3(r+1)\le p^r                                                \tag{43}
\]
holds for \(p\ge5,r\ge2\): it is immediate for \(r=2\), and induction follows by multiplying the right side by at least \(5\). Thus \(t<p^r\), so (36) and (37) apply. Let
\[
 v=v_p(t),\qquad f=v_p((t-2)!),
 \qquad \kappa=\#\{i:1\le i\le r,
 t\le p^i\}.
\]
The three factors in (41) respectively contribute at least
\[
 t,\qquad r-v,\qquad \kappa+r-f
\]
powers of \(p\). It remains to check
\[
 3(r+1)\le t+(r-v)+(\kappa+r-f).                             \tag{44}
\]

Here is the numerical verification. Since \(p\ge5\), Legendre's elementary bound gives
\[
 4f<(t-2).                                                    \tag{45}
\]
Also \(v\le\log_p t\). If \(t\le p^2\), then every \(i=2,\ldots,r\) is counted by \(\kappa\), so \(\kappa\ge r-1\). If \(t<p^2\), then \(v\le1\); if \(t=p^2\), then \(v=2\) and \(t\ge25\). In either subcase (45) gives
\(4+v+f\le t\), which implies (44).

If \(t>p^2\), put \(L=\lfloor\log_p t\rfloor\). Since \(t<p^r\), all indices \(L+1,\ldots,r\) are counted, so
\[
 \kappa\ge r-L.
\]
Moreover \(8L\le5^L\le p^L\le t\); the first inequality follows by induction for \(L\ge2\). Together with (45), this yields
\[
 3+v+f+L\le t.
\]
Using \(v\le L\) and \(\kappa\ge r-L\), this rearranges to (44). Therefore every term (41) has the required divisibility, and (40) is proved.

Exactly as in the first prime step, (40) extends from nonnegative \(B\) to every integer \(B\). Indeed, for fixed \(A\), the difference
\[
 U\bigl(p(p^rA),p^{r+1}B\bigr)-U(p^rA,p^rB)
\]
is an integer-valued polynomial in \(B\), of degree at most \(p^{r+1}A\). Apply the Newton expansion (22) with modulus \(p^{3(r+1)}\). We have therefore proved, for every integer \(B\),
\[
 U\bigl(p(p^rA),p^{r+1}B\bigr)
 \equiv U(p^rA,p^rB)\pmod {p^{3(r+1)}}.                     \tag{46}
\]

## 7. Completion of the proof

Let \(k\ge2\), and apply (46) with \(r=k-1\), \(A=n\), and
\[
 B=n(m+2).
\]
Since
\[
 np^k=p(p^{k-1}n)

a nd
\[
 (np^k)(m+2)=p^k n(m+2),
\]
identity (8) turns (46) into
\[
 A_m(np^k)\equiv A_m(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}.
\]
For \(k=1\), the same conclusion is (24).

Both indices \(np^k\) and \(np^{k-1}\) are positive. Thus the earlier discussion of the sole exceptional case \(m=-1\) applies: if one uses the quotient formula (2) with integer division, both values differ from the true values by the same constant \(1\), which cancels. For every other \(m\), the two definitions agree term by term. Hence (1) holds for the stated generalized sequence.

Finally, taking \(m=4\) gives
\[
 a(np^k)\equiv a(np^{k-1})\pmod {p^{3k}}
\]
for A333096, for every prime \(p\ge5\) and all positive integers \(n,k\), as required.
